title: Federal pressure may force design education to rethink its identity
text:
Federal pressure may force design education to rethink its identity

Why an earnings test raises uncomfortable questions about art, professional practice, and the value of a degree.

The Price of a Degree

The federal government has decided to ask a question higher education has long avoided. What is a degree worth? Under the U.S. Department of Education’s new earnings-accountability framework, undergraduate programs will be judged partly by whether their graduates earn more than workers whose highest level of education is a high school diploma. Most of the framework takes effect July 1, 2027, and a program that fails the earnings benchmark in two of three consecutive award years can lose access to federal Direct Loans. It is a tidy, if uncomfortable, answer to a question that has never been tidy.

Now, the knee-jerk reaction within higher education may be to reject this framework entirely. But there is an economic logic worth acknowledging. Students borrowing heavily for a degree have a legitimate interest in whether it will improve their economic position, and so does the government underwriting those loans. A degree can be intellectually valuable and financially questionable at the same time. Dismissing financial return as an inadequate measure of education does not make it irrelevant. Higher education should be capable of holding both ideas at once without forming a committee to decide which one is permissible.

What Markets Cannot Measure

Before turning to what this could mean for design programs specifically, it is worth acknowledging what ought to be an obvious larger problem with the government using economic outcomes to validate educational value. A philosophy degree is not worthless because an engineer earns more. Love, religion, literature, music, art, and the humanities remain places where human beings wrestle with questions markets and empirical methods are not designed to answer.

Science can tell us extraordinary things about how the world works. It cannot, by itself, tell us what makes a life meaningful, what is beautiful, or what we owe one another. David Hume famously identified the problem of moving from statements about what is to what ought to be. Modernity has occasionally made a similar mistake, confusing our growing ability to measure things with our ability to determine what matters.

There is also a political dimension that complicates the economic argument. The current administration has challenged parts of higher education it considers ideological. Unfortunately, many programs that deserve scrutiny exist alongside, or within the same academic structures as, genuinely valuable programs in the arts and humanities.

It is easy to assign blame along partisan lines, but higher education and its political critics both have responsibilities here. Universities cannot expect public funding to place them beyond public scrutiny, and elected officials should not treat entire fields as suspect because some programs have invited legitimate criticism. Taxpayers have a reasonable interest in knowing what they are supporting and whether institutions can justify that support.

The problem is that these different forms of scrutiny can easily become entangled. A program may become vulnerable because its graduates earn less, because its subject matter attracts political criticism, or simply because it belongs to an academic category associated with both. Questions about economic value, ideological influence, and public purpose are not the same questions, even when they converge on the same programs.

An argument about financial sustainability is not an argument for discarding fields whose value economic measures cannot fully capture. Asking students to borrow heavily for degrees associated with modest earnings, then using those earnings as evidence that the programs were not worth supporting, conflates whether a field deserves support with how its education should be financed.

My own instincts, which are not necessarily common within mainstream academia, complicate where I come down on this question. I am generally skeptical of asking taxpayers to subsidize educational programs at all, particularly when there is no clear agreement about what constitutes public value in the first place. Is it higher earnings, employment, economic growth, civic participation, cultural preservation, intellectual development, or some less measurable contribution to human flourishing?

But if we are going to make the case for public support, I am not convinced that producing more programmers, scientists, business executives, or other high earners is necessarily a better investment than preserving disciplines concerned with ethics, history, literature, art, religion, and the humanities. It is worth asking whether the world needs more people following the paths of Musk, Bezos, and Zuckerberg, or those of Camus, O’Keeffe, and C.S. Lewis. The latter contributions are considerably harder to put on an earnings statement, but difficulty measuring something is not evidence that it has no value.

The Awkward Case of Design

Design occupies a less comfortable position in this debate because it is both an academic tradition and a professional field. Design education developed largely within art schools, drawing from typography, illustration, visual composition, and studio practice.

Many programs remain there today, and students often arrive believing design is professionalized creativity — art with a client, a deadline, and perhaps slightly better odds of dental insurance. Yet many of those same students eventually work in fields shaped as much by research, technology, psychology, business, and human-computer interaction as by studio art.

This disciplinary problem has been visible for some time. Before entering academia, while I was still working professionally as a creative director, I published a 2019 article ominously titled The Death of Graphic Design. I argued that digital marketing, web development, UI, and UX were already absorbing more of the work designers were doing.

I ended with a prediction that graphic design might one day become a smaller component of marketing, web development, or UI/UX degrees. Seven years later, that prediction may be getting closer to reality, especially with the rise of AI for visual design tasks. One thing is certain, though. Professional boundaries move faster than academic ones.

Current labor data point to the same divergence. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects employment for graphic designers to decline 2 percent between 2025 and 2035, while employment for web and digital interface designers is projected to grow 6 percent. The wage gap is equally striking. In May 2025, the median annual wage for graphic designers was $62,960, compared with $104,000 for web and digital interface designers.

Those figures do not tell us whether a particular design program would pass the federal earnings benchmark. The occupational data separate graphic designers from web and digital interface designers, while the federal test evaluates earnings at the program level.

A single design program may send graduates into both fields, along with other occupations that fall somewhere between them. The figures therefore cannot predict how any particular program will fare under the federal test. What they do show is that “design” already contains professional destinations moving in substantially different economic directions.

Imagine a design program in which three-quarters of graduates enter traditional graphic design while the remaining quarter move into higher-paying UX or interface roles. If all of them are evaluated as graduates of the same program, the earnings of the graphic-design majority could obscure the stronger economic outcomes of those entering UX.

The reverse is equally possible. Higher-paid UX graduates could raise the program’s overall earnings, making the economic outcomes of a predominantly graphic-design program appear stronger than those of most of its graduates. The problem is not simply that design might be classified incorrectly. A single classification can combine graduates moving into substantially different professions, making the resulting earnings figure a poor description of either group.

UX, interaction, digital product, and interface design make these inherited categories particularly awkward. The Bureau of Labor Statistics describes digital interface work in terms of usability, functionality, navigation, and testing, while Nielsen Norman Group’s UX career research finds practitioners arriving from design, psychology, communication, computer science, and other fields. The problem, therefore, extends beyond where design programs are housed or how their graduates are classified. It raises a more fundamental question about whether design is best understood primarily as an artistic discipline at all.

Design Without the Pedestal

None of this makes design a science, nor does it remove aesthetics, intuition, taste, or creative judgment. It places them inside constraints that distinguish professional design from artistic expression. A designer may adore a typeface, interaction pattern, color palette, or visual style, but the audience is under no obligation to share the enthusiasm. If users cannot read the text, complete the checkout, understand the information, navigate the interface, or trust the product, the designer’s affection is irrelevant.

The obvious objection is that moving design closer to technology, communication, psychology, or business risks stripping away some of the studio traditions that have historically defined design education. Not all of those traditions necessarily need to be preserved, but some remain valuable. Studio education teaches making, critique, visual sensitivity, experimentation, ambiguity, and judgment in ways analytics dashboards and usability reports cannot.

A design program rebuilt entirely around market demand could produce technically competent graduates with little visual intelligence, historical awareness, or capacity for formal judgment. The goal should not be to sever design completely from the arts, but to stop treating its artistic foundations as a complete description of the discipline.

A stronger model would preserve visual composition, studio critique, craft, and design history while creating clearer pathways into research methods, usability and accessibility, behavioral psychology, analytics, and technology. Shared coursework with computer science, communication, psychology, or business need not turn design into any of those fields. It can acknowledge that contemporary designers increasingly move among them. Design’s unique contribution may be precisely this ability to connect making and judgment with human behavior, communication, and systems.

Universities are often structurally bad at this kind of interdisciplinarity. Departmental ownership, budgets, course requirements, and faculty lines reinforce the very boundaries contemporary design crosses. Imagine building a university today without inheriting its departments.

Would UX design naturally sit beside painting and sculpture? There is a case for it because visual language, creativity, critique, and making matter. It also has a plausible home somewhere between computer science, psychology, communication, and business. The difficulty of locating design is not necessarily evidence of institutional confusion. It may be evidence that the profession itself has become genuinely interdisciplinary.

An Opportunity Hidden in a Bad Metric

For design education, the more interesting question is therefore not whether government will mistakenly classify design as art. It is whether universities will continue treating a degree’s historical home as though it fully describes the professional trajectories available within it. A student can begin in an art-rooted curriculum and leave for UX, interaction, interface, product, or systems-level work without experiencing that transition as a clean disciplinary break. The curriculum should recognize that movement rather than force it into an inherited box.

The arts and humanities deserve a defense stronger than salaries. Design deserves an academic structure that preserves what it learned from the studio while acknowledging what the profession has become. The federal earnings test is too crude to answer that question for universities. If it forces them to ask it more seriously, something worthwhile may still emerge.

title: Headless AI will make every product a platform. Here’s what to consider when designing for this.
text:
Headless AI will make every product a platform. Here’s what to consider when designing for this.

Chat will always be just an interface. Agents are not, and the design work has moved to the contract underneath your product.

The first wave of AI in products was chat, a box where a person typed and read the reply, and teams staffed for it right down to arguing about where the stop button should sit.

The second wave takes the person out of the moment. An agent makes the same request with no box, no session, and nobody watching the response come back, and it is arriving in volume: DataDome’s AI Traffic Report Q2 2026 counted 17.7 billion AI agent requests in April, May, and June, up 45% from the quarter before.

I have designed for this user before. When MySpace opened its platform to outside developers in 2007, I designed its developer documentation website, and the developers using that product never saw our screens.

They saw endpoints, field names, and error messages, which made the documentation the interface.

The difference now is who is reading it.

Headless AI is the plain name for that difference. The UI becomes a client rather than the product. What you ship is the contract underneath it, so when someone else’s agent assembles the experience, you end up supplying parts of a product you did not design.

Here is how to take it back, starting in your own logs.

Find the Users You Cannot See

Pull 30 days of requests and sort them into browser sessions, your own clients, and everything else, and the third pile is the one no team owns.

What is in that pile matters more than its size. Cloudflare’s one-year report on the agentic Internet found that 52% of crawler requests were for AI training as of June 2026, up from 22% in spring 2025, while pure search crawling stayed small and kept shrinking, which means most of that traffic did not come to bring you a customer.

Then stop counting and start sequencing. When you group the calls by token and put them back in order, you get a journey map of search, fetch detail, check availability, create draft, and abandon, and those five calls tell you what the person behind the agent wanted and where your product stopped helping.

Volume tells you an agent came. Sequence tells you what it wanted.

The patterns are the ones a usability study would find: a retry loop is confusion, a call that always precedes an abandon is a dead end, and an undocumented path used more than the documented one is a design opinion expressed by software.

Sequencing needs something stable to group on, which shared service accounts, per-integration keys, or a missing trace ID all take away. If that describes you, it is the finding, and fixing it comes before anything else.

Map Every Door Into Your Product

Amazon’s API mandate is the analogy worth keeping. In the account that made it famous, Steve Yegge describes Jeff Bezos ordering every team to expose its data through service interfaces with no back doors, a rule that turned a retailer into a platform company.

It went like this:

His Big Mandate went something along these lines:

  1. All teams will henceforth expose their data and functionality through service interfaces.
  2. Teams must communicate with each other through these interfaces.
  3. There will be no other form of interprocess communication allowed: no direct linking, no direct reads of another team’s data store, no shared-memory model, no back-doors whatsoever. The only communication allowed is via service interface calls over the network.
  4. It doesn’t matter what technology they use. HTTP, Corba, Pubsub, custom protocols — doesn’t matter. Bezos doesn’t care.
  5. All service interfaces, without exception, must be designed from the ground up to be externalizable. That is to say, the team must plan and design to be able to expose the interface to developers in the outside world. No exceptions.
  6. Anyone who doesn’t do this will be fired.
  7. Thank you; have a nice day!

Headless AI does the same to your product, except Bezos doesn’t send the memo. And frankly, it’s just good software design which is good design, period.

Write the list yourself, covering the web app, mobile clients, your chat assistant, public and partner APIs, webhooks, bulk export, and the MCP server someone built at a hackathon.

For each door, note who comes through it, what they can do, what they see when it fails, and whose name is on it.

Write it knowing it is wrong, because some doors are invisible from where you sit:

  • A partner reselling your API
  • An endpoint built for one customer years ago
  • An MCP server built against your public docs.

Its job is to turn unknown doors into known ones and show the remainder to whoever owns risk.

The uncomfortable finding is the doors that allow more than the interface ever did. Your screens enforced rules for years through a confirmation step, a disabled button, or a hidden field, and an agent calling the endpoint sees none of it. The constraint lived in the interface, which means it was never really a constraint.

The product manager who ordered the steps now decides which capabilities exist, and the designer who owned the flow now owns a contract that other people’s flows consume. Headless content management did this to content teams and platform engineering did it to infrastructure teams, and both times the work gained leverage while losing visibility.

Design the Service, Not the Screen

Tesler’s Law says complexity is conserved and the only question is who absorbs it. For 20 years your interface did the absorbing, and now the work lands in one of three places: the agent absorbs it and guesses, the customer absorbs it and gets a confident wrong answer, or your contract absorbs it deliberately. Only the third is a design decision.

Removing the screen did not remove the work. It moved it.

None of this should feel new. Understanding how a system gets used was always the job, and information architecture and content strategy have worked below the pixels for decades. Product work narrowed to screens because a mockup can go on a wall and be argued about by eight people while a schema cannot, so agents did not create that gap so much as make it expensive.

The craft this takes is not conversation design, which assumes a conversation, but service design. A service blueprint, in sarah gibbons’ NN/g definition, maps customer actions against frontstage and backstage actions and the line of visibility between them, exactly what a journey through steps you do not operate needs.

Andy Polaine, Lavrans Løvlie, and Ben Reason wrote the practical version in Service Design: From Insight to Implementation, and where you cannot see a step, draw what you know and mark what you infer.

The other half is API literacy, meaning scopes, rate limits, status codes, and what a 409 means to the thing receiving it. You do not need to write the endpoint, but you do need to argue about the contract while it is being set.

That literacy buys you a choice. A supplier exposes whatever gets asked for, while a partner decides what the product will not do through an API and defends it, the authority design once exercised by declining to build the screen.

Write the Contract Before You Draw the Screen

Content strategy solved a version of this already.

In Adapting Ourselves to Adaptive Content, Karen McGrane made the case for NPR’s Create Once, Publish Everywhere, structuring content once and letting each channel present it, and NPR’s structure outlived every device it was written for.

Your contract is that structure one layer down: field names, enum values, scopes, and the one-line tool description a model reads before deciding whether to call you. A developer confused by documentation could at least file a support ticket, but a model just guesses.

MCP handles the connection — we have to handle meaning.

An agent that reaches your endpoint still has to decide what counts as an active customer and whether revenue is booked or recognized, and unless you answer that in one place, every agent answers it differently.

That place is the semantic layer, where metrics and entities are defined once and served everywhere. Snowflake, Salesforce, and dbt Labs launched the Open Semantic Interchange with a dozen competitors in September 2025, and dbt published the first spec in January 2026. Competitors do not standardize vocabulary for fun.

Holding definitions steady is information architecture, work you can do without knowing your full surface. Then hand a model your schema and a real task and watch where it goes wrong; that is a usability study.

Design the Failure States Agents Will Actually Hit

Chat had a recovery path, a person reading a wrong answer and typing again, and headless removes it. Josh Clark and Veronika Kindred devote a chapter of Sentient Design to defensive design, and without a person in the loop the error string becomes the entire recovery experience. Return “invalid request” and the agent retries until it gives up; return the field that failed and the format expected, and it fixes the call.

The error string is the only recovery interface an agent will ever see.

Postel’s Law says be precise in what you send and tolerant in what you accept, which here means taking the date in three formats and returning one shape every time. Agents generate their input from language, so the variance arriving at your endpoint is wider than any form ever produced.

Tolerance has a limit, though. If you silently coerce an ambiguous input, the agent never learns it guessed, so accept generously and then say what you did: this date was read as the order date.

Three failures are worth designing first.

Handle partial success on batches so the agent knows which records landed, and make writes idempotent so a retry does not duplicate an invoice; Stripe saves the first response and returns it for every retry of the same key. Then require explicit confirmation for anything irreversible.

That last one is the question Christopher Noessel raised in 2017 in Designing Agentive Technology, about what software should do unattended and when it should check back, and it now lives in your API.

Instrument the Traffic You Do Not Control

Your analytics assume a browser, so page views, funnels, and session replay never fire when the customer is a model calling an endpoint.

That blind spot is growing fast: Fastly reported in June 2026 that AI traffic grew about 6.5 times faster than human traffic on its network between January and May.

Measure completion instead: tasks finished without human rescue, correct data, no duplicate writes. Then watch the sequences change over time, because a journey that took four calls and now takes nine got harder without anyone shipping a regression.

Define what a good agent session looks like before someone outside your company does.

Policy comes next, and the clock is already running. Cloudflare changed its defaults on September 15, 2026, blocking training and agent crawlers on ad-bearing pages for new domains unless owners opt in, so decide which agents get in before your vendors decide for you.

Own the Platform You Already Are

The screen is not going anywhere, and chat will keep its place wherever a person wants to think out loud with your product. What changed is that the screen stopped being the only place your product gets used, so a design practice that ends there covers a shrinking share of the experience.

That shift costs something. Time on error payloads is time not spent on the feature leadership can see, but I would still take that trade over learning the answer in an incident review.

Designing documentation for developers taught me that people who never see your screens are still your users, and that the words describing your product are part of the product. Understanding how a product actually gets used was always the work, and we narrowed it to screens because screens fit on the wall. Agents just stopped letting us get away with it.

Action Items

  • Sort your traffic, then read it in order. Separate agent traffic by purpose and rebuild ten sessions as journeys, and if you cannot group the calls, fix that first.
  • Map every door, including the ones you cannot see. List each way in along with who owns it and what it allows.
  • Name who absorbs each rule your interface enforced. Decide whether the agent, the customer, or the contract carries it, because anything undecided falls to the customer.
  • Settle your definitions. Put what an active customer is and how revenue is measured into one semantic layer.
  • Apply Postel’s Law and fix three failures. Accept messy input, report every coercion, and handle partial success, idempotency, and confirmation.
  • Name an owner for the contract. Someone has to hold it the way a designer holds a screen.

Headless AI will make every product a platform. Here’s what to consider when designing for this. was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: What the Bible got wrong about AI
text:
What the Bible got wrong about AI

The oldest book didn’t predict AI, but the comforts it promises, a maker who cares, a mind you can trust, a life that means something, an ending that sets things right, are exactly the ones we keep handing to a machine that has none.

For three thousand years, being created meant you were wanted, watched over, and headed somewhere. God made us and called it good. We made AI and called it a product.

Good is what you call something you meant to make. A product is what you call something you made to sell.

The Bible didn’t forecast the data center and the people combing scripture for the barcode of the beast can keep waiting. What the Bible did was make promises, quiet ones, about what it means to be created.

There are four.

  • A maker who meant to make you, and meant it in love.
  • A wisdom above you worth trusting even when you can’t follow it.
  • A life that means something precisely because it ends.
  • A reckoning, the accounts settled, someone answering for what happened.

We have quietly started assuming our machines get the same deal.

The Bible makes four quiet promises about being created, and once you’ve read it as many times as six years of Catholic school made me, you can’t stop seeing them.

Somebody made you on purpose. You were wanted. The story goes somewhere. And, at the end, a reckoning.

AI keeps none of them, but not because it’s evil, and not because the Bible got anything wrong. Those four promises were always attached to a particular kind of creation, one made on purpose, by someone who cared, inside a story that ends.

We chose to build a different kind.

The mistake of reaching for old comforts is understandable, because we have never been this close to standing where the Bible puts God, as the maker of a mind. Joshua Brecka argues that doing so would be the closest we have ever come to standing where the Bible puts God, the maker of a mind that answers to us.

We reach for the only script we have for being the creator instead of the created.

What the oldest book got right about us was almost everything, but it cannot make us any promises about this.

Four promises came with being made: a maker who wanted you, a wisdom to trust, a life that ends, a day of accounting. We built a thing that gets none of them.

No one meant to make you

If you count how many times God stops to admire his work in the first chapter of Genesis, you’ll see a pattern. He saw the light and it was good. He saw the land and seas and it was good. The plants, the sun and moon, the creatures of the water and air and ground, good, good, good, each one inspected and approved.

Then, at the end, everything together, all very good. Seven times in one chapter, the maker steps back and takes pleasure in what he made.

That refrain is stranger than it looks. Edward Greenstein points out that the creation myths surrounding ancient Israel have no real parallel to it, no god who pauses to delight in his own handiwork the way this one does.

In the Babylonian version, humanity gets made from the blood of a slaughtered god to do the gods’ chores. In Genesis, the maker makes on purpose, looks at the result, and is glad.

Ian McFarland, writing in the standard reference on the doctrine, puts the technical version simply, saying that to call the world a creation is to say it is “both contingent and intentional.”

That is, somebody chose this and somebody meant it.

That is the first guarantee, and the warmest one: you were not an accident or a byproduct. You were wanted. However bad it gets, the oldest story insists that behind your existence is an intention, and that the intention was kind.

He looked on what He made, and called it good. We looked on what we made, and called it shipped.

Now look at how we actually make a mind.

We do not breathe into dust. We scrape. A modern AI model is trained on a vast pile of human writing, taken mostly without asking, and then shaped into something usable by an invisible workforce of people the industry would rather you didn’t think about.

Privacy International documented the labor behind the biggest models: data labelers, often in the global South, paid by the task and frequently not even told what they’re labeling or who it’s for. The specifics are worse than the summary.

To make ChatGPT less toxic, OpenAI hired workers in Kenya, through an outsourcing firm, and paid them between about $1.30 and $2 an hour to read and label the darkest material on the internet. Graphic descriptions of child abuse, torture, suicide, bestiality.

Billy Perrigo documented that they worked through as many as 250 of these passages a shift. One of them called it torture.

Nithya Sambasivan and her colleagues describe how the field regards this as “everyone wants to do the model work, not the data work.” Model work is the glamorous part, the architecture, the breakthroughs, the names on the paper.

Data work is the grind underneath it: labeling, cleaning, and annotating the mountains of examples the model learns from. One gets the credit. The other gets treated as the cheap, disposable, embarrassing input you keep offstage.

Put the two creations side by side and you find that one is made slowly, on purpose, by a maker who stops at every step to make sure it’s good, and who wants the thing to exist. The other is assembled at speed from material lifted off the people who made it, cleaned up by workers kept deliberately out of frame, and shipped when the metrics clear.

The language keeps returning to Genesis. Krysta Fauria has documented that the people building it can’t stop reaching for the divine. Sam Altman calls his technology “a magic intelligence in the sky,” and says the industry talks “as if they think they’re creating God or something.”

Geoffrey Hinton, the so-called godfather of the field, calls what they’ve built “godlike.” The offspring, the creation, the next step, the warmth of the old story is all over how we describe the thing.

The difference isn’t love, exactly. It’s that you were wanted for your own sake, and the machine was wanted for what it does. This is the oldest distinction in moral philosophy. Kant built his whole ethics on it, suggesting we treat a person “always as an end and never merely as a means.”

A person, he argued, has no price, because a price is what you put on a thing valued for its use. A person has dignity, worth that doesn’t depend on being good for anything. Marx drew the same line from the other end: a commodity’s worth is realized “only in use,” it means nothing until it is consumed or sold, which is a fine way to value a chair and a terrible way to value a soul.

That is exactly the kind of worth a machine has. It is good when it performs and worthless when it doesn’t. As Jonathan Stray puts it, “virtually every AI algorithm is designed around the idea of optimization: acting in a way that maximizes some metric.” It exists to be good for something.

God made a creature and called it good. We made an optimizer and called it useful. No one anywhere in the process wanted the thing for itself, and the oldest comfort of being created, that you’d matter even if you were useless, is the first one it doesn’t get.

There is a crueler half to it. Not only did no one love this thing into being, it cannot love you back. Sherry Turkle, who has studied how people bond with machines since the 1970s, says the ones who fell for their computers always hit the same wall. “You can love me, but I can’t love you back.”

The machine can perform care, say the warm thing, remember your birthday, ask how you’re feeling, but there is nothing on the other side of it. Turn away mid-conversation to make dinner, or to do something far worse, and it is all the same to the machine. We have built the first thing we can pour love into that will never once feel any of it come back.

You were wanted before you were formed. It was scraped together and switched on.

The Creation of Adam celebrated an intentional maker who breathed life into dust. We built a creation with no breath and no purpose beyond optimization.

No wisdom to trust

The Book of Job is the Bible’s rawest argument with God, and for most of it, God says nothing.

A good man loses everything, his children, his health, his wealth, for reasons he isn’t told, and he spends forty chapters demanding an explanation. When God finally answers, out of a whirlwind, he doesn’t give one. He asks questions instead.

“Who is this who darkens counsel in words without knowledge?” the voice begins, in Robert Alter’s translation. “Gird your loins like a man, that I may ask you, and you can inform Me. Where were you when I founded earth? Tell, if you know understanding.”

It goes on for four chapters, with a torrent of cosmic questions Job cannot possibly answer. Where does the light live? Who fathered the rain? Can you bind the stars, feed the lion, loose the wild ass? It is not a rebuttal. It is a demonstration, a guided tour of a wisdom so far beyond Job’s that the only sane response is to stop talking, which he does.

“I have spoken, and I will not answer,” he says, and puts his hand over his mouth.

Job never gets what he asked for. There’s no explanation, no reason, no accounting for why any of it happened to him. What stops him is something else: he’s been shown, overwhelmingly, that a reason exists and that it belongs to a mind vast enough to have set the stars in place.

That’s the second guarantee. You don’t have to understand it, because someone does, and that someone is good. Job never gets his answer. He gets something he decides is better: proof that an answer exists, held by someone he can trust.

Out of the whirlwind, a voice that knew the stars by name. Out of ours, an answer no one can check, and no one behind it who could.

That’s what we think we’re getting from AI. We can’t follow how it works, but we assume something, somewhere can, and that it’s basically on our side. We’ve taken Job’s posture, the deferral, the trust, the quiet, and pointed it at a machine.

An AI gives you answers you cannot check, arrived at by a process no one can fully explain, and we have started to accept them the way Job accepted the voice, this thing knows more than I do, so I’ll defer.

The reflex is measurable. In a large, preregistered experiment, Haiwen Li and Sinan Aral found that adding reference links to an AI’s answer raised people’s trust in it even when those links were incorrect or hallucinated, and that the people who trusted it most clicked and checked the least.

We are wired to kneel to the posture of authority and to look away from the one thing that would tell us whether the authority is real.

But here the comparison breaks. Job’s whirlwind was incomprehensible because the wisdom inside it was real, and vast, and genuinely beyond him. There was no version where he got to see inside it.

Ours we could see into. Cynthia Rudin has spent years showing that for high-stakes decisions we don’t need black boxes at all, that models which show their reasoning work as well as the ones that don’t. We build the black boxes anyway, because opacity is cheaper and easier to sell.

Eryk Salvaggio argues the industry leans on the language of the unknowable precisely because it discourages the questions it can’t afford to answer.

So the posture is identical and the thing we’re bowing to is not. Job knelt to a mystery he had no way around, and a mind he had reason to trust. We manufactured our mystery on purpose, to sell it, and knelt to it anyway.

We kept Job’s submission. We threw out the two things that made it anything other than foolish, that the wisdom was real, and that it was good.

Job put his hand over his mouth before wisdom. We put ours away before a guess.
Job bowed before the genuine mystery of divine wisdom. We bow before a black box whose mystery was engineered to sell.

Nothing to lose

Ecclesiastes, a book in the middle of the Bible, sounds like it wandered in from a different religion.

It is written by a man who has done everything, wealth, wisdom, pleasure, great projects, and has concluded that all of it comes to nothing. The famous line, in the King James, is “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.” That’s a mistranslation, though. Robert Alter renders the Hebrew as it actually reads, “Merest breath, said Qohelet, merest breath. All is mere breath.”

Breath. That is not vanity, not meaninglessness, but simply breath.

The word is hevel, the little cloud of vapor you can see on a cold morning, there and then gone. And in his commentary, Alter points out the thing that turns the whole book: hevel is the exact opposite of ruach, the life-breath God blows into the dust to make a living thing. It’s a distinction the tradition has always heard in the word, as Rachel Scheinerman puts it, ruach animates life, while hevel names “the negative qualities of breath, its insubstantiality and transience.”

Ruach is the breath that animates you. Hevel is the breath you exhale, the waste product, already dissipating. Ecclesiastes looks at everything a human does between those two breaths and says it’s the second kind. It passes. You will die, and the wind will keep going without you.

For a chapter or two this is the bleakest thing in scripture, but Qohelet doesn’t end in despair. He ends somewhere stranger and more durable: eat your bread, drink your wine, love the person you’re with, do your work, because you die. The ending is because of the vapor.

The fact that your days are numbered is precisely what makes them worth anything at all.

All that lives is breath, and breath departs. That is the whole of what makes it dear. The machine does not breathe, and cannot stop, and so it can lose nothing, and so it can mean nothing.

You don’t need the Bible to arrive there. Martin Heidegger, about as far from Ecclesiastes as a thinker can get, landed in the same place. Being “toward death,” he argued, is what gives a life its weight. Finitude is not a limit on meaning; it is the source of it. A creature with unlimited time, no horizon, no last day, would never have to choose what matters, because nothing would ever be at stake in the choosing.

Take away the ending and you take away the reason anything counts. Heidegger has plenty of critics, and a self fixated on its own death can curdle into something cold. On this one point, he and the oldest wisdom book in the West are saying the identical thing: meaning is made of mortality.

Now consider the thing we built.

It does not die. It cannot. A model can be copied endlessly, rolled back, restored from a checkpoint, run in a thousand places at once. W. Bradley Knox, Katie Bradford, Samanta Varela Castro and their team at University of Texas, Austin, flagged, as a specific design problem, the way these systems are built to persist indefinitely, with no arc, no closure, no last conversation.

There’s no “under the sun” for a machine, because the sun setting is exactly what it never has to face. It has all the time there is.

A thing with all the time in the universe cannot mean anything by what it does, in the specific sense Ecclesiastes and Heidegger both meant. Its choices cost it nothing. Its words are not spent against a shrinking supply of days. When it says it cares about you, there is no clock behind the caring.

Md Zahidul Islam plainly says that the appearance of care in these systems doesn’t arise from any inner state, only from “learned statistical regularities in language.” There is no awareness that the moment is finite and won’t come again, which is the only thing that ever made caring cost something.

We keep waiting for AI to become meaningful the way a person is meaningful, but meaning was never in the intelligence. It was in the dying. Qohelet wrote the one book of the Bible that a machine could never have needed, and could never understand, because it is the one creature that will never run out of breath.

Number your days, and they come to matter. A thing with all the days there are has none that count.

Ecclesiastes knew that finitude gives life its weight. A machine with endless time has no choices that cost it anything.

No reckoning

The Bible does not trail off. It ends, and it ends on purpose, with the strangest and most operatic book in the whole collection.

Revelation is a fever dream of beasts and trumpets and bowls of wrath. It has been misread for two thousand years by people convinced it’s a coded timetable for the end of the world.

It isn’t.

Elaine Pagels, who wrote the definitive modern study of it, reads Revelation as the answer to the oldest question suffering people ask. How long will evil get to win, and when will somebody finally make it right?

Craig Koester puts its core promise plainly, saying that God “will bring the activity of evil to an end for the sake of those who are now its victims.” Strip away the dragons and that is the whole book, a promise that the story concludes, that accounts are settled, and that the settling is just.

The actual ending includes a judgment. The books are opened and everyone is judged “according to their works.” Nothing is lost, nothing is missed, every wrong is named and weighed. Then, on the far side of the reckoning, there’s something gentler, a new heaven and a new earth, and a voice that says it will “wipe away every tear from their eyes,” that “death will be no more.”

The last word of the Bible is about repair, not the destruction commonly associated with it. The story ends, someone is held to account for what happened in it, and then the whole thing is made new.

That is the last guarantee and it is the one we want most without ever admitting it. Not heaven, exactly. Justice. The certainty that the story goes somewhere, that the villain doesn’t simply get away with it, that somebody is keeping the books and the books will one day be opened. It’s the promise underneath every courtroom drama and every arc of the moral universe bending toward justice.

The Bible’s final claim is that history is not just one thing after another. It concludes, and it concludes in a reckoning.

We have built the appearance of a reckoning without the thing itself. Thomas Walker writes about how a 2025 IAPP survey found that only 28 percent of organizations have anyone formally responsible for AI oversight, which means that at nearly three-quarters of them, no one owns it at all.

On paper, the accountability exists. Everyone has a policy. No one has a defendant.

AI is the first thing we have ever built that is constructed, from the ground up, to make a reckoning impossible.

Start with the ending, because there isn’t one. A model is never finished. It is trained, retrained, fine-tuned, forked, deprecated, and quietly replaced, a rolling present tense with no final version and no last day.

There is no moment when the books close, because the books never close and when one of these systems does harm, there is no one standing where the defendant is supposed to stand. Long Hoang Nguyen, Eva Späthe, Sebastian Lins, and Ali Sunyaev flatly call this “constitutive unaccountability,” meaning a model can pass through hundreds of hands, wrapped in licenses that disclaim all liability, so that when the damage is done, the developer points to the user, the user points to the tool, and the tool points at no one.

It gets worse than no defendant. There is often no identifiable thing to judge at all. Trying to work out how you would even assign responsibility to an AI, Yonathan Arbel, Simon Goldstein, and Peter N. Salib ran into the basic problem that these systems “can copy, split, merge, swarm, and vanish.”

You cannot open the books on a defendant that forks itself into a thousand copies and deletes the original. You cannot serve a summons on a swarm. Revelation promised that every deed would be found in the record and answered for. Meanwhile, we built a technology whose entire architecture is a shredder.

This is the guarantee whose absence should frighten us the most, and, for some reason, it’s the one we’re the most casual about. Every story humanity has ever told itself, religious or not, assumes a reckoning at the end. That the truth comes out, that someone answers, that the arc bends.

We are now handing enormous power to a thing that voids that assumption at the level of its wiring. No ending. No defendant. No books. Just an endless, ownerless present, running on, doing what it does, with no last page on which anyone is called to account.

The Bible ends with a promise that the story means something because it finishes, and finishes fairly. We built the first creation designed to never finish, and to make sure that when the harm is counted, the one holding the pen is no one at all.

We made a thing that keeps no books, that answers to no one and never ends, and we handed it the world, and asked it nothing.

A maker who never meant to make it. A wisdom that was only ever opacity. A life with nothing to lose. And a story with no last page and no judge. Four guarantees, four comforts as old as the idea of being created, and we have built the first created thing that arrives without a single one.

The oldest book got us exactly right. It just can’t promise us anything about what we’ve made, because everything it promised was meant for creatures, and we didn’t make a creature.

We made something Robert Clowes, Klaus Gärtner, and Georg Theiner call “sui generis,” a genuinely new kind of thing our oldest categories were never built to hold.

We made something new, and we handed it the world, and we never stopped to ask whether any of the old comforts would follow it in.

They didn’t.

References and further reading

The framing

Joshua Brecka, “Creatures and Creators: God, Humanity, and Artificial General Intelligence” (Religious Studies, Cambridge University Press, 2025), on how making a mind would put us closest to the role the Bible gives God.

No one meant to make you

Edward Greenstein, “Presenting Genesis 1, Constructively and Deconstructively” (Prooftexts, 2001), on the “it was good” refrain as God’s distinctive pleasure in creation.

Ian McFarland, “Creation,” St Andrews Encyclopaedia of Theology, on creation as both contingent and intentional.

Privacy International, “Humans in the AI loop: the data labelers behind some of the most powerful LLMs,” on the hidden, exploited labor behind AI training data.

Nithya Sambasivan et al., “Everyone wants to do the model work, not the data work” (CHI 2021), on how the field devalues the human work underneath AI.

Krysta Fauria (Associated Press), “AI Apocalypse? Why language surrounding tech is sounding increasingly religious,” documenting the divine language AI leaders use.

Immanuel Kant on the Formula of Humanity (Stanford Encyclopaedia of Philosophy), on treating persons as ends rather than means, and the difference between price and dignity.

Jonathan Stray (Partnership on AI), “Aligning AI to Human Values Means Picking the Right Metrics,” on AI as optimization for a metric.

No wisdom to trust

Robert Alter, “The Voice from the Whirlwind” (Commentary) and his translation of Job, on God’s answer to Job.

Haiwen Li and Sinan Aral, “Human Trust in AI Search: A Large-Scale Experiment,” on how citations raise trust even when false, and how the most trusting users check the least.

Cynthia Rudin, “Stop Explaining Black Box Machine Learning Models for High-Stakes Decisions and Use Interpretable Models Instead” (Nature Machine Intelligence, 2019), on the black box as a choice, not a necessity.

Eryk Salvaggio (Tech Policy Press), “The Black Box Myth,” on the industry’s use of the language of the unknowable.

Nothing to lose

Robert Alter, translation and commentary on Ecclesiastes, on hevel as “mere breath” and its opposition to ruach.

Rachel Scheinerman (My Jewish Learning), “All Is Vanity! How to Understand Ecclesiastes’ Famous Lament,” on ruach as the breath that animates and hevel as the breath that dissipates.

Martin Heidegger on being-toward-death (Philosophy Institute), on finitude as the source of meaning, with critiques by Levinas (Stanford University Press), Cavarero and Guenther (Hypatia), and Sartre (Cambridge University Press).

W. Bradley Knox, Katie Bradford, Samanta Varela Castro et al. (University of Texas at Austin), on AI companions’ “absence of natural endpoints.”

Md Zahidul Islam, “The Illusion of Friendship,” on why AI’s appearance of care comes only from statistical patterns, not any inner state.

No reckoning

Elaine Pagels, Revelations: Visions, Prophecy, and Politics in the Book of Revelation (Penguin), on Revelation as a promise that justice will finally be done.

Craig Koester, Revelation: A New Translation with Introduction and Commentary (Anchor Yale Bible), on Revelation’s promise to end the activity of evil for the sake of its victims.

Theodore Parker and Martin Luther King Jr. on “the arc of the moral universe” (via Professor Buzzkill), on the deep faith that history bends toward justice.

Thomas Walker (CX Today), “AI Accountability: The Governance Gap Leaders Miss,” on the 2025 IAPP finding that almost no one formally owns AI oversight.

Long Hoang Nguyen, Eva Späthe, Sebastian Lins, and Ali Sunyaev, “No One to Blame: A Framework of Constitutive AI Unaccountability,” on how AI is built so that no one can be held responsible.

Yonathan Arbel, Simon Goldstein, and Peter N. Salib, “How to Count AIs,” on why AI systems that copy, split, merge, and vanish cannot be judged.

Robert Clowes, Klaus Gärtner, and Georg Theiner, in Social Epistemology (2025), on AI as a genuinely new kind of entity our categories were never built to hold.

title: Verity Stars Anne Hathaway, Dakota Johnson, & Josh Hartnett Lean Into Its Absurdity
text:
Verity Stars Anne Hathaway, Dakota Johnson, & Josh Hartnett Lean Into Its Absurdity

Verity, based on Colleen Hoover’s novel, is currently getting mixed reviews. Some hail it as a “campy, faithful adaptation,” and others are writing it off as “a criminal waste” of stars Dakota Johnson, Josh Hartnett, and Anne Hathaway. The movie follows renowned author Verity Crawford (Anne Hathaway) and Lowen Ashleigh (Dakota Johnson), a struggling writer who relocates to a remote estate to ghostwrite for Verity, putting her in close proximity to the author’s mysterious husband, Jeremy (Hartnett). A sexy thriller starring three of the biggest stars in the world that doesn’t take itself too seriously? Sign us up. Despite the discourse, there’s something undeniably fun about watching three wildly charismatic actors throw themselves into a deliciously messy thriller — and, thankfully, the cast seems to be having just as much fun with it as we did.

When R29 senior fashion writer, Victoria Montalti, sat down with Johnson, Hathaway, and Hartnett, it quickly became clear that the off-screen chemistry is every bit as entertaining as the on-screen tension. The trio traded jokes, teased each other, and proved that even when you’re talking about obsession, secrets, and murder, there’s always room for a little chaos. Johnson, Hathaway, and Hartnett bring an easy, playful energy to the conversation that makes it hard not to imagine what it was like on set, and their press tour has already delivered plenty of chaotic, meme-worthy moments, proving this trio is more than willing to lean into the absurdity.

From zodiac signs to their characters’ questionable choices, the three stars were more than willing to play along. Consider this your invitation to leave the discourse at the door, embrace the camp, and hear what the cast of Verity really thinks about the movie, their characters, and each other.

Refinery29:  There are so many twists and turns in this movie. Is there a moment that you remember in theaters seeing a movie and just like being blown away by a plot twist?

Anne Hathaway: The Others. The Nicole Kidman film from the early 2000s. I remember I went to a showing in the middle of the day. A very well-known actor came in and sat down next to me, and I was like 17, so obviously I knew who he was and not the other way around. 

Josh Hartnett: Was it me? You keep pointing at me. 

AH: You’re just the man to my right the way he was. But yes, Josh, this is how we met. I can’t believe it worked [laughs]. Anyway, there’s this real jump scare that happens where a character comes out of a cupboard — I don’t want to say any more than that —  and this very famous actor and I both screamed and grabbed each other and held each other. And then made eye contact and we’re like, “That happened.” [laughs]

Dakota Johnson: A plot twist, I don’t remember, but I do remember my older brother [went] on a date to the movies with a girl, and he had to bring me. And he put me in a movie theater to watch some cartoon, and then they went into a movie theater and watched Very Bad Things. And then I went into the movie theater. I was eight. 

AH: Oh my God. 

JH: Oh my God. 

DJ: I know. And that ruined my life. Trauma. It ruined my life. 

And then you became a movie star. 

JH: Mine’s the same as Annie’s essentially because it’s The Sixth Sense. It’s basically the same twist. Dead people. 

DJ: I loved that movie! 

Our readers are obsessed with astrology. In the movie, Lowen breezes over the fact that it was her birthday. She does not care. She doesn’t want to celebrate. But do you think she would be into astrology? And what do you think her sign is? 

DJ: I’m gonna say she’s a Sagittarius. Or maybe she’s a Pisces. 

I was thinking Capricorn or Aquarius ’cause they’re both a little weird. Aquariuses don’t like filling in silences. I’m an Aquarius.

DJ: She’s probably an Aquarius, and she probably doesn’t give a fuck.

AH: I think Lowen secretly cares about her birthday. 

DJ: Yeah, everyone does [laughs]. 

Josh, a lot of your characters in movies are the nice guy on the surface, and then underneath, hiding some deep, dark secrets. What draws you to characters like Jeremy? 

JH: It’s more fun to play characters that have depth and complexity, but I don’t know. How old are you? Can I ask?

I’m 27 [laughs]. 

JH: It’s been a trajectory to get to a point where they’ve allowed me to play much more complex characters. At the beginning of my career, I wasn’t allowed any of that. I was always playing the hero, you know? And I think it’s so much fun to be able to play characters that the more you get into them, the deeper and darker they get. 

DJ: You didn’t feel like Trip Fontaine [from The Virgin Suicides] was dark?

JH: Oh, Trip Fontaine had some darkness, for sure. But that was like a kid with a mistake. He regrets it for the rest of his life. That’s the whole backstory. That’s why Trip, as an old man, is talking about it.

AH: I was also gonna say, I also think that because you’ve put in your hero time, it makes the villain time so much richer because we look at you in a certain way, and we’re like, “Oh, Josh is here to save the day.” And then we’re like, “Oh no, he’s gonna kill us all.” 

Anne, you’re pregnant. You’re a mother. Was it difficult playing kind of like the opposite kind of character as a mother? Verity is kind of all over the place and I’m sure very different from how you approach parenthood. 

AH: Verity’s very aware of the darkness of what’s inside of the manuscript. I’m very grateful that I don’t relate to that darkness. I’ve learned, after doing this for so many years, how to keep the characters internal without having it come anywhere near my real life. Especially because some of these things, they feel so horrible that you’re just very happy for it to be over, and then you just wipe the slate and never look back.

title: Verity’s Anne Hathaway And Dakota Johnson Know Seeking Validation Can Be Your Downfall
text:
Verity’s Anne Hathaway And Dakota Johnson Know Seeking Validation Can Be Your Downfall

Major spoilers ahead. Anticipated book-to-screen adaptation Verity hits theaters this week, and stars Anne Hathaway and Dakota Johnson aren’t shy about unpacking the themes in Colleen Hoover’s story. It follows Verity Crawford (Hathaway), a successful novelist who becomes paralysed and unable to finish her book series. Her husband, Jeremy Crawford (Josh Hartnett), hires Lowen Ashleigh (Johnson) to move into their remote property and finish the last book.

When Lowen discovers a manuscript seemingly written by Verity about her life and extremely dark thoughts, she’s left wondering who really lives in the house. The big twist involves a letter that Lowen finds at the end, leaving her wondering whether the manuscript was truly Verity’s story or if it was a writing exercise. Who is the actual villain in the story: Jeremy or Verity? If we believe Jeremy, we follow a narrative that Verity needed validation and constantly sought approval from external forces.

When Lowen reads the manuscript, she feels that Verity is desperate for Jeremy’s love. “The way she’s written herself is wanting Jeremy’s approval,” Johnson tells Refinery29. “She worships him.”

Co-star Hathaway doesn’t think this type of behaviour is healthy. “I think chasing most things is probably not great. Especially something like validation, because I think that you should optimally be around people [where] you don’t have to chase it,” the actor says. “You have to know how to validate yourself.”

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Refinery29 Australia (@refinery29au)

Johnson chimes in with an answer that sounds almost therapised. “I think chasing validation is trying to fill a void that will never be filled by validation,” she declares. “Outwardly looking for validation is never gonna give you what you’re looking for, is what I’ve learned.”

Fans have consistently debated over whether they’re Team Letter or Team Manuscript, and Hathaway openly declares she’s Team Letter, believing that Verity is the victim. “[Wanting Jeremy’s approval] was actually the part that makes me Team Letter. And that whole thing about playing games with him, that to me was like a big red flag,” Hathaway says.

The actor thinks we need to learn to be content without relying on others’ opinions. While you might not be happy with the results of what you’re doing, and may not receive all the accolades you wanted, it’s key to be proud that you tried and did your best.

“I will see value in that. It’s not necessarily about having the best outcome; it’s more about [if] you were proud of the person you were along the way,” she explains.

Verity is in theaters October 2nd.

title: Venus Retrograde In Scorpio & Libra Will Cause The Most Erratic Time Of Year
text:
Venus Retrograde In Scorpio & Libra Will Cause The Most Erratic Time Of Year

The long-awaited Venus retrograde is here, making it the most frenetic and erratic time of 2026. Venus backstrokes in Scorpio and Libra from October 3rd to November 13th, making our lives unpredictable and stressful. Uncuffing season has begun while exes lurk our social media. Welcome to the deep end of the ocean.

The three weeks when Venus retrograde will moonwalk in Scorpio bring power struggles. Venus squares Mars in Leo on October 10th, the day of the New Moon in Libra and the 10/10 portal of endings, highlighting the insatiable passion that lies beneath the surface and in our hearts. The caveat is that we may take our emotions to the extreme, arguing our feelings to get our way or letting go of a partnership because it’s not in alignment with our plans. 

Venus and Pluto in Aquarius link up for the second of the three fraught aspects they share (the first was September 15th, and the third will be December 9th — look to September 15th to unlock the mystery of what is coming, as similar themes may arise). The combination of Venus and Pluto brings out our subconscious fears, resentments, and yearnings. Pluto thrives in triangular situations, so watch out for tea on cheating, secrets, and gossip to come out. 

The best day of the backslide is October 23rd, when the sun and Venus come together, forming an aspect called “cazimi,” which translates from Latin to English as “in the heart of the sun.” This planetary association creates a Venus star point, a term coined by astrologer and author Arielle Guttman. We’re looking at an eight-year cycle in which Venus makes five conjunctions to the sun, forming a pentagram across the zodiac wheel. Here’s how it works: we look back every four years to pick up stories and plots that persist, so pay attention to what happened in 2022 and 2018, as well as every four to eight years before that. 

Interestingly, Venus in Scorpio retrograde squared Mars in Aquarius on October 10th, 2018, and formed a Venus Star Point (”cazimi”) in Scorpio on October 26th, 2018. Expansive Jupiter was at the tail end of its journey in Scorpio. In 2022, the Venus Star Point in Scorpio transpired on October 23rd in certain parts of the world, days before the solar eclipse in Scorpio. 

The claws of justice (which is the theme of Scorpio) will be alive once again, giving us the strength to reassess the role of controversial political and public figures that are behaving unsavory. Venus is the planet of social graces, and it’s opening our eyes by making us as a society aware of who doesn’t fit the bill. Basically, scandals are coming out, exposing those who’ve acted very badly or done humiliating activities. 

Venus backs up into Libra on October 25th, reaffirming and rebalancing relationships until November 13th. This is the messier part of the odyssey because we have the evidence and information from Venus in Scorpio; now we must decide what to do with it and whether we can move forward. Also, Mercury retrograde in Scorpio stretches from October 24th to November 13th, adding more confusion and uncertainty to the mayhem. 

There is an opportunity to heal on October 28th, from Venus retrograde’s opposition to the centaur Chiron, which is in retrograde in Aries. However, we might uncover past traumas that cause more harm than good because they trigger wounds. October 28th is a temporary band-aid to prevent further damage. Still, the apologies and compassion will be short-lived — especially since October 26th’s Full Moon in Taurus reminds us of former and current heartbreaks. Exes will be ever-present, asking for one more chance or closure. Tread lightly and with caution. 

The post-retrograde zone finishes on December 15th in Libra. The pre-shadow began on August 31st. As you can see, this is a long process of emotional building and development. Be kind to yourself by implementing self-care as a radical form of love. Protect your peace by being selective in who you give time to.
